bh1: It was a winter night. No one had any idea what was about to happen.
In the north of the city stood Union Carbide's pesticide plant.
Tank number 610 held 42 tonnes of methyl isocyanate. An extremely toxic gas.
Late at night, water got into the tank. The pressure kept rising.
And after midnight, this poisonous gas escaped into the night air.
The gas was heavier than air. It flowed along the ground and crept into sleeping homes.
bh2: That night, the night shift was on duty in the plant's control room.
At around 11 pm, the pressure in tank 610 began to rise.
It is believed that while pipes were being washed, water reached the tank.
The refrigeration system that kept the tank cool had been shut down since June, to save money.
The flare tower that burned off gas was down for repair. And the scrubber was on standby.
Every safety barrier had already failed.
Workers turned on the water curtain. But the water could not reach the height of the stack.
bh3: People woke up to the sting of the gas.
Burning eyes, struggling to breathe. No one understood what was happening.
People ran out of their homes just as they were.
Thousands were on the streets. No one knew where to run.
Many ran with the wind, straight along with the gas cloud.
The gas was heavier than air, and it was filling the low-lying areas.
Those who ran towards higher ground had a better chance of surviving.
Carried by the wind, the poisonous cloud spread over the whole old city.
And the city got no warning in time.
bh4: The railway station was caught by the gas too.
Hundreds of passengers were on the platform. Many collapsed where they stood.
An express train, full of passengers, was standing at the platform.
If it had stayed, the people on board would have been trapped in the gas too.
On duty that night was the deputy station superintendent, Ghulam Dastagir.
The gas was making him sick as well. Still, he did not leave his post.
Without waiting, he sent the train off ahead of time.
And he warned the other stations that no train should come to Bhopal.
bh5: By morning, thousands of people had gathered outside Hamidia Hospital.
Some carried their children, some held up their parents.
The hospital corridors filled with patients lying on the floor.
Doctors and nurses had been working nonstop all night.
The doctors did not even know which gas it was, or how to treat it.
They kept rinsing burning eyes with water, and did whatever they could.
In the first few days alone, tens of thousands of people needed treatment.
But many people never even made it to the hospital.
bh6: When morning came, there was a strange silence in the lanes.
The belongings of those who had fled in the night lay scattered where they fell.
Slippers, bundles, bicycles. As if everything had suddenly stopped.
On the streets lay people who would never get up again.
By then, the gas cloud had moved on.
In about two hours, nearly 40 tonnes of poisonous gas had mixed into the air.
Thousands of animals died too. The leaves on the trees turned yellow and fell.
In a single night, Bhopal had changed forever.
bh7: For days afterwards, pyres kept burning at the cremation grounds.
Firewood ran short. Often, several people were cremated on a single pyre.
In the graveyards, graves were dug in rows.
Every faith, every neighbourhood had lost its own.
According to the government, 3,787 people died.
By other estimates, more than 8,000 people died in the first few weeks alone.
More than 500,000 people were affected by the gas.
And the deaths went on for years.
bh8: 7 December. Union Carbide's chairman, Warren Anderson, arrived in Bhopal.
He was arrested right at the airport.
He was held under house arrest at the company's own guest house.
But within a few hours, he was released on bail.
He was flown out of Bhopal on a state government plane.
After that, he never returned to India.
The court declared him an absconder. But he never appeared in court.
In 2014, he died in the United States.
bh9: 14 February 1989. A settlement was reached in the Supreme Court.
Union Carbide paid 470 million dollars. And the case was considered closed.
The victims were never even asked. They took to the streets.
Their question was: is a human life worth only this much?
And even that, only after years of waiting.
7 June 2010. A Bhopal court delivered its verdict.
Seven former officials got two years in prison. And bail the same day.
bh10: After the disaster, the factory shut down. But the poison stayed.
Hundreds of tonnes of toxic waste lay there for years.
For years, chemical waste had been dumped into ponds next to the factory.
With every rain, this poison slowly seeped into the ground.
The hand pumps and wells in the nearby settlements became poisoned.
People kept drinking the same water. Because there was no other way.
Forty years later, in 2025, the waste was finally removed.
But the poison under the ground is still there today.
bh11: The poison did not stop with that night. It reached the next generation.
In gas-affected families, many children were born with illnesses.
Doctors recorded more cases of birth defects.
Rehabilitation centres were opened for these children.
Today, a new generation is growing up in the same settlements.
Children on their way to school hear of that night only in stories.
Children play in the shadow of the factory wall.
On land whose poison has still not been washed away.
bh12: Those who had lost everything did not give up.
Women like Rashida Bee and Champa Devi Shukla led this fight from the front.
Survivors walked about 800 kilometres, from Bhopal to Delhi.
So that their voice would reach the nation's capital.
Their demands were simple. Clean water, medical care, and justice.
In 2004, these two women won the Goldman Prize.
Every year, on 3 December, Bhopal lights candles.
For those who never came back after that night.
bh13: A statue stands in front of the factory. A mother holding her child to her chest.
It was made in 1985 by the Dutch sculptor Ruth Kupferschmidt.
On the walls around it, the victims' stories are painted in colour.
These walls do not let the city forget.
A small museum keeps the belongings of those who died that night.
Slippers, clothes, utensils. Every object, a story.
Beneath the statue it says: No Hiroshima, No Bhopal.
bh14: After Bhopal, India made new laws.
In 1986, the Environment Protection Act came into force.
Around the world, safety rules for hazardous factories became stricter.
Alarms, emergency plans, and people's right to know.
Today's Bhopal is a city of lakes.
More than two million people live their lives here.
But the world's worst industrial disaster is a warning.
Human life can never be cheaper than profit.
bh15: Today, evening still settles over Bhopal's lakes just as it always has.
The city has moved on. But some wounds never heal.
The factory's skeleton still stands in the dark.
Like a silent witness to that night.
Thousands of people died in a single night. Hundreds of thousands still carry its burden.
For them, justice is still incomplete.
Remembering Bhopal is not just history.
It is a promise that this will never happen again.
